text: also be used as a prophylactic measure.4,7,17,21 Calcium supplementation has a small but positive effect on BMD and tends to reduce the incidence of vertebral fractures. Low vitamin D status has been associated with reduced BMD, and increased risk of falls and hip fracture in eld- erly people; however, differences in baseline vitamin D concentrations make comparison of studies difficult.8 Vitamin D supplementation appears to reduce the risk of hip and non-vertebral fractures,7,8 especially in those with vitamin D deficiency. Excessive vitamin D should be avoided, as this may decrease BMD.2 Studies of sup- plementation with calcium plus vitamin D show equiv- ocal results on fracture rates.8 However, daily calcium with vitamin D supplementation is recommended for elderly institutionalised people with limited exposure to sunlight.15,16,18 • Bisphosphonates are antiresorptive drugs that are used first-line for the treatment and prevention of osteoporo- sis.4,15,16,20 While aminobisphosphonates and non-nitro- gen-containing bisphosphonates differ in their effect on BMD,14,23 no comparative studies have been done and BMD changes do not necessarily correlate with fracture reduction;23 some consider effect on fracture rates to be similar.14 There is good evidence that alendronate or risedronate, given orally, can prevent bone loss,4,11 improve BMD,1,4,6 and reduce the risk of both vertebral and non- vertebral fractures.1,2,8,9,13,21 These effects are seen with- in 1 year of starting treatment,24 and effects on BMD persist for some while after stopping the drug, particu- larly with alendronate.14 Evidence for other bisphos- phonates is more patchy: oral or intravenous ibandro- nate,11 and intravenous pamidronate6 or zoledronate1,11 have all been shown to increase BMD at the spine and hip. Oral ibandronate has been shown to decrease verte- bral fracture risk in women with osteoporosis, as well as non-vertebral fracture risk in those with severe dis- ease.11,25 Intravenous ibandronate has been associated with a reduction in the incidence of new fractures.11 In a controlled study,26 a once-yearly infusion of zoledronate given over a 3-year period significantly reduced the risk of vertebral, hip, and other fractures. BMD at the hip, femoral neck, and lumbar spine also increased signifi- cantly compared with placebo. Oral cyclical etidronate has been shown to decrease the risk of vertebral frac- tures,1,3 (as has oral clodronate17), but evidence for an effect on non-vertebral fractures is less clear.17 In the UK, NICE27 recommends the use of bisphosphonates for the secondary prevention of osteoporotic fragility fractures in postmenopausal women.
